5.7 Returning After the Fire Note: This section presents general considerations for dealing with ash and chemicals. It is not intended to replace advice or assessments from professionals or agencies directly involved in cleanup activities. Even after the worst of the fire and smoke is over, individuals who return after the fire should be aware of health and safety hazards. Public health officials should work closely with officials from affected counties to warn residents of health and safety concerns during cleanup and to provide information on best practices for homeowners returning after a fire. This may include creating a list of reputable cleanup or debris removal businesses. 119

Exposure to lingering smoke and ash can cause significant health effects in both healthy individuals and those in at-risk groups. People may experience symptoms including respiratory irritation, heat-related illness, and emotional stress after a fire. Physical stress from cleanup activities, exposure to toxic chemicals, damaged power lines, and equipment such as portable generators can cause injuries during cleanup. Ash from burned structures in the wildland-urban interface (WUI) may contain traces of hazardous substances such as metals (including arsenic, lead, copper, nickel and chromium); asbestos from older buildings; caustic materials; and other chemicals (Plumlee et al. 2007, Villarruel et al. 2024). It is therefore advisable to be cautious and avoid exposure to the ash. In addition, the burned material itself may pose a hazard. For example, products that contain lithium-ion batteries, like electric vehicles, wheelchairs, power tools, game controllers, and other everyday items, can re-ignite, explode, or emit toxic gases if exposed to wildfire. Before beginning cleanup work, it is important to ensure structures are safe to enter, assess the level of cleanup needed, and develop a plan for who will perform the cleanup and how. Professional assistance should be considered if there is structural damage or hazardous materials are present,

to ensure structures are safe to enter, assess the level of cleanup needed, and develop a plan for who will perform the cleanup and how. Professional assistance should be considered if there is structural damage or hazardous materials are present, the HVAC system is impacted, or the scale of cleanup is more than the affected individual can manage on their own. Additionally, smoke often accumulates at the highest level of a home or building. People with attics should consider working with a professional to assess potential impacts to insulation and other materials. FEMA’s Homeowner’s Guide to Risk Reduction and Remediation of Residential Smoke Damage provides guidance on remediating smoke damage in homes, including tips for selecting a contractor and documenting damage for insurance purposes. People returning to their homes for cleanup activities should consider the following: • • • • If the presence of asbestos, lead, carbon monoxide or other hazardous material is suspected, do not disturb the area. Dust masks or filtering facepiece respirators do not protect against asbestos or gases such as carbon monoxide. Avoid handling burned items that may contain hazardous chemicals, such as cleaning products, paint, and solvent containers. Do not touch fire-damaged products with lithium-ion

Avoid handling burned items that may contain hazardous chemicals, such as cleaning products, paint, and solvent containers. Do not touch fire-damaged products with lithium-ion batteries. They should be considered extremely dangerous, even if they look intact. If devices emit popping or hissing noises or are actively smoking or on fire, do not attempt to extinguish or smother the battery. Leave the area immediately, move upwind at least the length of a football field (330 feet) and call 911. Do not start, move, tow or charge a fire-damaged electric/hybrid vehicle or use or start a firedamaged residential energy storage or house battery until it has been assessed and deemed safe by a hazardous material professional. 120

Avoid ash from wooden decks, fences, and retaining walls pressure treated with chromated copper arsenate (CCA) as it may contain lethal amounts of arsenic. Avoid stirring up or sifting through ash if possible; ash deposited on surfaces can become inhaled if it becomes airborne during cleanup. For example, avoid using leaf blowers or dry sweeping. Instead, mist hard surfaces with water before sweeping or mopping. Clean all carpets and soft goods such as couches, mattresses, pillows, pet beds and plush toys using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filtered vacuum, if available. Wash homegrown fruits and vegetables. Dispose of ash in the regular trash. If hazardous waste, including asbestos, is suspected to be in the ash, contact local hazardous waste authorities regarding appropriate disposal. Individuals performing cleanup work should wear protective clothing and equipment, such as a well-fitting NIOSH Approved® N95 ® respirator, leather gloves, safety glasses or goggles, long pants, a long-sleeved shirt, and shoes with rugged soles. Individuals temporarily relocating to a new residence during the cleanup of their home should be advised against transporting any ash-covered or smoke-exposed items in their vehicle or to their temporary residence, to reduce exposure. If it is necessary to transport any items contaminated by ash, they should be placed into a plastic bag while wearing gloves and seal the bag completely before placing it in a vehicle. Smoke and ash residue can impact air quality in affected structures. Depending on the severity of smoke intrusion into the building and the duration of exposure, some people may notice visible deposits of smoke and ash residue and/or a lingering odor when they return to their homes, schools, or workplaces. Removing smoke odor is difficult, but there are ways to diminish it, beginning with cleaning and thoroughly airing the structure (Laguerre and Gall, 2024, Li et al., 2023). Every surface of the space exposed to smoke or ash may require cleaning, depending on the extent of the impact. The amount of damage can be assessed with a walk-through of the affected structure checking for visual evidence of smoke and ash residue (e.g., using a white cloth or wipe to check for deposits on surfaces) and smelling for smoke odor. People should be advised to consider seeking professional cleaning or discarding items that are difficult to clean. WUI fires that burn human-made materials can emit chemicals that can be detrimental to health. Chemicals in smoke can deposit on outdoor surfaces and infiltrate into homes. In these cases, consider recommending that household 121

materials such as carpets and upholstery be discarded, especially if there is direct evidence of hazardous contaminants depositing on indoor or outdoor spaces. Cleaning includes wiping down the walls, floors, windows, baseboards, doors, frames, cabinets, furniture, and other surfaces. Cleaning using dry methods, wet methods or a combination of both may be appropriate, depending on the surface. Follow manufacturer’s instructions when available. Dry methods, such as vacuuming and using sticky rollers or “soot” or “chem” sponges, generally work well for thick deposits of ash and porous materials. Dry sweeping and dusting are not recommended. When vacuuming, a HEPA vacuum is preferred, if available. If a HEPA vacuum is unavailable, features that make a vacuum more suitable for ash cleanup include true HEPA filters on the exhaust and a sealed system that ensures air passes through the filter. A typical household vacuum or a shop vacuum will send some of the collected dust or ash out into the air. If using these, consider wearing a respirator and using techniques to remove ash and pollutants from the air such as increased ventilation or indoor air filtration. Wet cleaning methods, such as damp wiping or mopping, often work well for light deposits and non-porous materials. A dilute solution of water and soap is usually sufficient for wet cleaning. Some people may choose to use additional cleaning products; however, note that some cleaners may also impact indoor air quality. Note that while mechanical air filters remove fine particles in the air, they do not remove the gaseous chemicals that cause odors associated with wildfire smoke. These chemicals must be removed by using a PAC with an activated charcoal filter or a filter composed of alumina coated with potassium permanganate. Most portable air cleaner filters for gaseous compounds become saturated quickly and lose effectiveness in smoky environments. They will need to be replaced frequently. PACs with more 122

robust odor removal are available but are frequently expensive. This is why thoroughly cleaning the home interior to remove sources of off-gassing volatile organic compounds (VOCs) is so important. In general, avoid using products that add chemicals to the indoor environment to remove or neutralize smoke odors. The use of an ozone generator to remediate smoke odor is not recommended because ozone can create as many problems as it is intended to fix. Many of the chemicals that are broken up by ozone can produce byproducts that are also dangerous to health. Furthermore, ozone does not remove ash and other particles from the air and indoor surfaces. If an ozone generator is used to remove smoke odors, it should be used only by a remediation professional. The space where the ozone generator is used must be unoccupied during use and for a designated period after use to ensure that no one is exposed to ozone. B.1 Introduction When wildfires occur, smoke can impact a wide range of distances, depending on the amount of fire emissions, how high they are lofted into the atmosphere, and the particular meteorological conditions and transport winds. When dealing with wildfire smoke, it is important to consider not only current air quality conditions, such as: • Where is current air quality being impacted? • What have the trends and patterns been over the past several days? but also, to assess fire information: • Where are the fires and how big are they? • How much are they expected to grow? as well as smoke transport downwind: • • • Where are smoke plumes being observed? Where do smoke models say smoke will go over the next few days? Are there diurnal patterns for the smoke impacts? B.2 When Looking at Air Quality Conditions B.2A Considerations Considerations when looking at air quality conditions depend on whether the goal is to determine the current prevailing conditions or to extrapolate recent observed patterns into a prediction for the future, whether the data being used is remotely sensed (e.g. by satellites) or based on ground observations, and what kind of devices are being used to collect the data. Satellite and data fusion products: Satellite based representations of air quality generally show total air column or tropospheric conditions rather than ground concentrations, or ground concentrations are extrapolated based on statistical relationships. Data fusion products incorporate both satellite and ground-based data to create smooth fields of air quality concentrations at the surface. Such products are inherently more accurate close to ground observation locations, in areas away from strong sources of smoke, and in areas with more open terrain. Ground observations using monitors and sensors: Ground-based observations of air quality generally fall into 3 types: (1) established permanent monitoring sites, where siting, maintenance, and quality control are handled by established agencies and owners; (2) rapidly deployed temporary monitoring equipment put out by agencies such as the federal U.S. Interagency Wildland Fire Air Quality

3 types: (1) established permanent monitoring sites, where siting, maintenance, and quality control are handled by established agencies and owners; (2) rapidly deployed temporary monitoring equipment put out by agencies such as the federal U.S. Interagency Wildland Fire Air Quality Response Program (see Chapter 1) and state agencies like the California Air Resources Board; and (3) lower cost air quality sensors that may either be owned and deployed by agencies and skilled community groups, but also may be owned and operated by private citizens with unknown training. Each source type has tradeoffs as listed in Table B1. 126

For example, diurnal patterns showing the worst time of day and best time of day are often relatively stable over several days under a consistent weather pattern and fire growth. Trends showing increasing or decreasing impacts of smoke as well as increasing or decreasing

showing the worst time of day and best time of day are often relatively stable over several days under a consistent weather pattern and fire growth. Trends showing increasing or decreasing impacts of smoke as well as increasing or decreasing areas of impact can also be useful. However, to utilize these patterns, additional knowledge is needed. To utilize diurnal trends, knowledge of whether the meteorological patterns are continuing to follow the past several days is needed; if there is a frontal passage moving through that will typically disrupt diurnal patterns. To utilize trends both an understanding of the stability of the meteorological patterns as well as an understanding of how fire growth has progressed and what fire growth is expected to happen moving forward is needed. Trends in air quality conditions are often directly related to trends in fire growth, as fire emissions are, to a substantial extent, directly related to fire growth. 127

B.3 When Accessing Fire Information B.3A Considerations Considerations when accessing fire information include how a recent fire of interest started, how the fire information is being gathered, what the inherent or system-specific delays on that information are likely to be, and what kinds of biases may be inherent to the specific types of information being gathered for display. Generally, fire information falls into 3 types, each with its own characteristics: (1) information from observations and reports by the incident command team (IMT) working the fire (see Chapter 1); (2) information from automated satellite systems that can detect fire hotspots; and (3) information on planned activities by the management team, such as a planned burnout of unburned fuels. Progression of fire information sources: It’s often difficult to obtain information about brand new or emerging wildfires and good information from ground reports may take a day or two (or longer) to become available. Until then, the best way to get ground observations about a new wildfire may come as news reports or social media posts as well as automated satellite based remote sensing. Once a wildfire grows to the point that local fire response agencies can no longer manage it, an Incident

about a new wildfire may come as news reports or social media posts as well as automated satellite based remote sensing. Once a wildfire grows to the point that local fire response agencies can no longer manage it, an Incident Management Team will be ordered which will then start feeding information into state and/or national incident response databases. Source type and timing: Information from an IMT and planned activities are generally input by humans and therefore can have greater value due to the data sources’ ability to integrate and assimilate information into a coherent narrative. However, the timing of such information usually lags more automated fire tracking from satellites. Reports from IMTs may be up to multiple posts daily to delayed by up to a few days. Reports from IMTs may also include adjusted fire perimeters from ground observations and from aircraft operations. Automated fire hotspot detection is generally available within 1-3 hours of the observation. Fire growth: Satellite hotspots are indicative but not an accurate measure of the amount of fire growth of a fire. Issues with assessing fire growth from hotspots include the pixel size of the imagery of the satellite system which range from approx. 375m to

are indicative but not an accurate measure of the amount of fire growth of a fire. Issues with assessing fire growth from hotspots include the pixel size of the imagery of the satellite system which range from approx. 375m to several kilometers. Satellites typically cannot reliably record whether the fire has consumed all of part of a pixel creating uncertainty in their fire growth estimates. Additionally, the ability of a satellite to observe the fire can be compromised by heavy clouds and/or smoke which sometimes means that satellites will observe no growth (no hotspots detected) during particularly smoky fire growth days. 130

B.4 When Viewing Smoke Plume Extents B.4A Considerations Considerations when viewing a smoke plume extent include how the smoke plume extent was determined and therefore what it represents, the timing of when the smoke plume extent was created, and the relationship of the smoke plume extent with smoke concentrations on the ground. Smoke plume extents are generally derived from satellite observations, from a smoke dispersion model, or from a data fusion product that combines the two. Smoke plume extents are rarely determined from actual observations of ground level air quality as air quality measurements are generally too sparse to generate detailed maps. In some urban areas it is possible to use measurements due to the large number of air quality sensors in the area allowing the creation of detailed progression maps of smoke plumes through the community. Smoke plume extents as Figure B1. Smoke from many large fires creating haze across the western and central United States. Red dots are satellite fire hot spot detections (NASA WORLDVIEW, September 4, 2017). To learn more, see the NASA Worldview Tutorial by the NASA Health and Air Quality Applied Sciences Team (HAQAST) at https://haqast.org/nasa-tools. determined from satellites are created by automated algorithms based

satellite fire hot spot detections (NASA WORLDVIEW, September 4, 2017). To learn more, see the NASA Worldview Tutorial by the NASA Health and Air Quality Applied Sciences Team (HAQAST) at https://haqast.org/nasa-tools. determined from satellites are created by automated algorithms based on various kinds of satellite imagery, by combinations of automated systems and human quality control checking, and, where necessary, human-drawn smoke plumes. A constellation of satellites operates in different Earth orbits, providing different combinations of temporal and spatial coverage. Global observations come from polar orbiting satellites, meaning measurements are collected on 14 pole-to-pole orbits with a field of view of Earth below that shifts ~2600 km each orbit. Depending on the instrument, measurements directly beneath the satellite might be as fine as 30m or more commonly coarser (500m-5000m). The coarser measurements – combined with multiple side-by-side measures – allows for global coverage once per day whereas the finer resolution instruments typically require multiple days or multiple satellites to achieve full coverage. In geostationary orbit, a satellite orbits the Earth at the same rate as Earth rotates, so that the focal area on the ground is consistent. At the focal area (e.g., the continental United States, northern Mexico and Southern Canada),

coverage. In geostationary orbit, a satellite orbits the Earth at the same rate as Earth rotates, so that the focal area on the ground is consistent. At the focal area (e.g., the continental United States, northern Mexico and Southern Canada), the instrument can rapidly repeat measurements at high spatial resolution. The 133

combination of similar instruments in polar- and geostationary-satellites provides global coverage with higher frequency in focal areas and enables cross-platform verification where the two overlap in time and view. Smoke plumes determined by satellites usually represent total air column smoke rather than ground level smoke as satellites generally are most capable of detecting the overall opaqueness of the surfaceto-space air column they are looking through. This can create a good picture of how smoke in one area is connected to the source in another area, because the plume is being tracked no matter what elevation in the atmosphere it travels. It is most easily thought of as tracking where, if you look up, will the sky be orange or hazy as some elevation above you? However, this total air column smoke plume is logically disconnected from what is generally of most concern which is what the smoke concentrations are at the ground. Even “heavy” total air column smoke plumes – representing significant opaqueness of the total air column as detected by the satellite – may not reach the ground or affect air quality to communities. “Heavy” satellite plumes can often be coupled with “GOOD” air quality levels as measured on

representing significant opaqueness of the total air column as detected by the satellite – may not reach the ground or affect air quality to communities. “Heavy” satellite plumes can often be coupled with “GOOD” air quality levels as measured on the ground. Think of an orange sky above but no smell or effects from smoke at the surface. Other considerations for satellite derived smoke plumes include clouds and timing. High clouds can obscure satellite detects of smoke plumes. Clouds are distinguishable from smoke plumes by color (clouds are brighter white) and character and both human and automated systems generally are fairly good at making the distinction. Satellites can only detect smoke plumes during the day as they require reflected light. This means that satellite smoke plumes are not available at night and depending on when the overpasses and/or analyses are scheduled, may not be available until mid-morning. Fog can be another confounding factor which may be marked as smoke on these displays. Smoke plume extents as determined by smoke models or by data fusion products generally try to capture ground level smoke extents. However, some of these products also produce a total air column smoke plume extent to compare to

these displays. Smoke plume extents as determined by smoke models or by data fusion products generally try to capture ground level smoke extents. However, some of these products also produce a total air column smoke plume extent to compare to the satellite smoke plumes as discussed above. Therefore, when viewing smoke model or data fusion smoke plumes it is important to check what variable is being shown. Smoke model and data fusion smoke plumes generally are produced on regularly timed intervals. Satellite observations range from detailed color images that are intuitively valuable to quantitative estimates. Satellites measure light from a variety of sources and different colors. Active satellite instruments measure light that they emit and are less common than passive instruments. Passive satellite instruments measure reflected solar radiation, human lights, or other thermal energy. Anything that relies on direct solar radiation is limited to making measurements during daylight hours. Images of the earth during daylight hours can be reconstructed from measured light of different colors, and are useful for seeing fires, smoke, and plume transport. Analysis of these images is typically qualitative and requires interpretation. For example, the NOAA Hazard Mapping System smoke polygons are hand drawn based on these

measured light of different colors, and are useful for seeing fires, smoke, and plume transport. Analysis of these images is typically qualitative and requires interpretation. For example, the NOAA Hazard Mapping System smoke polygons are hand drawn based on these images. Satellites can also measure specific colors (spectral bands) which can be used to identify the power emitted from fires or burned areas. Fire power and burned areas are 134

important datasets to estimating air quality emissions from fires. Aerosol optical depth is another measure, which uses reflected solar radiation to measure particulate matter in the atmosphere. Go-kit (Oregon OEM checklist) Medications and medical devices · glasses · food and plenty of water · important documents · phone chargers · battery AM/FM radio · first-aid kit · flashlight · N95 masks · long sleeves, long pants, sturdy shoes, hat. Plan two routes out. Move livestock early.

Around the house (defensible space) - First 5 ft around the house: nothing that burns. Firewood and lumber 30 ft away. - Within 100 ft: grass mowed to 4 in or less, 10 ft between tree crowns, limbs 10 ft from the chimney, no "ladder fuels" (brush under trees). - Clean roofs and gutters; cover vents with 1/8-inch metal mesh; clear around propane tanks; keep the driveway clear enough for a fire engine.

Smoke Make one cleaner-air room (windows shut, AC on recirculate). A DIY air cleaner = a box fan (made 2012 or later, UL/ETL label) + a MERV-13 furnace filter. Unplug it when you leave the house. Use N95 masks outdoors. Details: the Wildfire\ folder (Ready-Set-Go guide, OSFM defensible-space guide, OSU fire-resistant plants, EPA/OHA smoke sheets). Fire news: swofire.com (ODF Southwest Oregon).

🌎 Earthquake (Cascadia) and tsunami - A Cascadia magnitude-9 quake would shake for 4–6 minutes, with aftershocks for months. Drop, Cover, Hold On. - Expect landslides on mountain roads and damage to bridges. Coast-to-inland routes like US-199 are exactly the kind expected to be cut, so the valley may be isolated for a long time. - State estimates for inland western Oregon: power out 1–3 months, water/sewer 1 month to 1 year, main highways 6–12 months to partly reopen, fuel shortages (Oregon's fuel hub is near Portland). - Plan to be on your own for at least 2 weeks — longer in rural areas. - At the coast (Brookings, Gold Beach, Crescent City): if you feel a long quake, walk to high ground immediately. The first waves can arrive in 15–30 minutes; surges continue 12+ hours and the first is not the largest. Details: Earthquake-Tsunami\ (Living on Shaky Ground, 2 Weeks Ready toolkit, Cascadia scenario, tsunami evacuation maps for Brookings-Harbor, Gold Beach, Crescent City, Smith River).

🦌 Hunting and 🎣 Fishing While seasons and tags are still enforced, the 2026 rule booklets are in Hunting\ and Fishing\ (the 2027 big game and fishing booklets come out around December 2026 — see Keeping this current). With or without rules, the units, waters and seasons below tell you where game and fish are, and when — and leaving breeding animals and spawning runs alone is what keeps them there next year. Hunting units: US-199 is the line. West of the highway (Illinois River canyon, Kalmiopsis) is Chetco Unit 27 (82% public land). East of it (Lake Selmac, Takilma, Oregon Caves, Williams) is Applegate Unit 28 (57% public land). In Cave Junction, Kerby, Selma and O'Brien, which side of the highway you're on decides the unit. North of the Rogue at Grants Pass is Evans Creek Unit 29. 2026 general seasons, for orientation (check the current booklet): western Oregon buck rifle Oct 3–Nov 6 · archery deer & elk Aug 29–Sep 27 · Unit 28 coast elk rifle Nov 14–17 and Nov 21–27 (Unit 27 is controlled hunts only) · black bear Aug 1–Dec 31 · cougar all year (quotas) — bear and cougar must be checked in at ODFW within 10 days · grouse and quail Sep 1–Jan 31 · fall turkey Sep 1–Jan 31 · spring turkey Apr 15–May 31. Chronic wasting disease has not been found

🪤 Trapping How-to: start with the national Trapper Education Manual and the NY trapper manual (trap types, baits, water and land sets, snares, running a trapline, fur handling), then the species guides (beaver, coyote, raccoon, bobcat, gray fox). For improvised traps with no store-bought gear, see the 1907 Deadfalls and Snares (illustrated) and the snare and deadfall chapters of the Army survival manuals (Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals). Hides and furs: USDA Home Tanning of Leather and Small Fur Skins. - Check traps at least daily — animals spoil, suffer, or get taken by other predators. - Beaver, raccoon, muskrat and rabbits are the most dependable meat from traps here; wear gloves for rabbits and rodents (tularemia), and cook all wild meat thoroughly. - Don't catch your own dogs: the AFWA dog-friendly guides show sets that avoid pets. While Oregon's rules are still enforced (details in the 2026–2028 furbearer booklet in Trapping\): - License: trapping needs an Oregon Furtaker's License — that includes "unprotected" animals like coyote, skunk, opossum and porcupine. A landowner can get a free license for land they own and live on (register the land with ODFW first). - Trapper education (free, online at hunter-ed.com/oregon/trapper) is required if you were born after June 30, 1968 or are trapping in Oregon for the first time — except on your own or family land, or when controlling damage to livestock or crops. -

after June 30, 1968 or are trapping in Oregon for the first time — except on your own or family land, or when controlling damage to livestock or crops. - Every trap and snare must carry your ODFW brand number. Check traps at least every 48 hours. - Banned: toothed jaws; oversized footholds and land killing traps (size limits are in the booklet); game meat as bait; visible bait within 15 ft of a foothold set for carnivores. In the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest west of I-5 (that includes the Illinois Valley), no traps or snares hung in trees. On public land, stay 50 ft from trails and 300 ft from trailheads, campgrounds and picnic areas. - 2026–27 seasons: bobcat Dec 1–Feb 28 (needs a record card) · gray fox Oct 15–Feb 28 · raccoon, river otter and beaver Nov 15–Mar 15 · mink and muskrat Nov 15–Mar 31 · marten closed west of I-5 · fisher and ringtail closed all year. - Wolves are federally endangered here. Use coyote traps no bigger than #3 and snares with breakaways. A wolf track is about 5 in long; a coyote's is about 2.5 in. Report any wolf caught by accident right away: ODFW, US Fish & Wildlife (503) 231-6179, or OSP (541) 664-4600.

💧 Water - Store at least 1 gallon per person per day for 2 weeks, plus water for animals. - To treat questionable water, bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute, or use plain unscented household bleach as shown in the dosing table in Water\EPA - Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water. - After a flood or wildfire, shock-chlorinate your well and have it tested (OHA and OWRD sheets in Water\). Rainwater collection rules for Oregon are in Water\ too.

⚡ Off-grid power and creek hydro Start with the US Navy NEETS modules (electricity basics, AC, circuit protection, wiring, generators) in Off-Grid-Power\Electrical-Basics, then the solar guides, then the micro-hydro handbooks in Off-Grid-Power\Micro-Hydro. Generators - Never run one indoors, in a garage, crawlspace or shed, even with doors open. Carbon monoxide kills in minutes. Keep it outdoors, away from windows and vents, and use battery-powered CO alarms. - Never plug a generator into a wall outlet ("backfeeding"). It sends power back through the lines and can kill anyone working on them. Wire into the house only through a transfer switch. - Store fuel outside living areas, in proper cans. Let the engine cool before refueling. Sizing a solar system (Sandia and IEA guides) - Panel size (kW) ≈ (kWh you use per day ÷ peak sun hours) × 1.2. - Lead-acid batteries: count on only 40% of the rated capacity. At our latitude, plan 7–9 days of storage for a solar-only system, and vent battery rooms at the top (hydrogen rises). - System voltage: 12 V under 1 kWh/day, 24 V for 1–4 kWh/day, 48 V above that. Low voltage over long wires needs very heavy wire. Sizing creek hydro (NRCan, NCAT) - Real output (watts) ≈ flow (liters/second) × drop (meters) × 9.8 × 0.5. In US units: kW ≈ flow (cubic ft/min) × drop (ft) ÷ 709 × 0.5.

NCAT) - Real output (watts) ≈ flow (liters/second) × drop (meters) × 9.8 × 0.5. In US units: kW ≈ flow (cubic ft/min) × drop (ft) ÷ 709 × 0.5. Example: 50 gallons/minute falling 100 ft ≈ 470 W around the clock ≈ 11 kWh a day, more than solar gives most of the year here. - Design for late-summer low flow (the flow you have 95% of the time). Size the pipe so friction eats less than 10% of the drop. Screen the intake and leave water in the creek. - A hydraulic ram pump (Clemson plans) lifts creek water uphill with no fuel or power. While Oregon's water laws are enforced: hydropower needs a state water right, and most Illinois Valley creeks are closed to hydro by state rule, including the Illinois River and its forks, Althouse, Sucker, Deer, Josephine, Rough and Ready and many more (OAR 690-515-0050). The OWRD guides and forms are in Micro-Hydro\.

🧼 Homestead skills: soap, fuel, heat, sanitation, crafts Everything is in Homestead-Skills\ — start with the short Practical Action briefs (illustrated, step by step), then the longer manuals. For everyday necessities — cleaners, laundry soap, tooth powder, fire starters, oil lamps, glue, mending, tire sandals, pads and diapers — see the Make-Do Household Guide in this folder. Firewood (OSU, heat per cord when dry): Oregon white oak and madrone ≈ 30 million BTU, Douglas-fir ≈ 21, alder ≈ 18, ponderosa pine ≈ 17. Each 1% of extra moisture costs about 1% of the heat: split and stack wood through one dry summer (two is better) and keep it covered through the rains. A good stove is 60–80% efficient; an open fireplace 10–15%. Carbon monoxide kills. Never run a generator, grill, charcoal, camp stove or a wood-gas unit indoors, in a garage or near windows. CO feels like flu without a fever. A battery CO alarm near the bedrooms is cheap insurance. A wood-gas generator keeps making CO-rich gas for ~20 minutes after the engine stops. Lye (for soap and biodiesel): wear gloves and goggles, keep children away, add lye to cold water a little at a time (never water to lye), never use aluminum pots. On skin or in eyes: flush with lots of water for a long time (not vinegar). Methanol (for biodiesel): very flammable, vapors creep along the

lye), never use aluminum pots. On skin or in eyes: flush with lots of water for a long time (not vinegar). Methanol (for biodiesel): very flammable, vapors creep along the ground to flames, absorbed through the skin, and swallowing it causes blindness. Work outdoors, away from any flame. Stored fuel: gasoline stays good about 6 months (longer with stabilizer), diesel 6–12 months. Approved cans, outside the house, in a tub to catch spills. Sanitation is what keeps disease away when water and sewer stop: the OSU twin-bucket toilet, then a proper latrine (Army FM 21-10, the WHO notes) at least 100 ft downhill from any well or creek, and handwashing with soap every time. While laws are enforced: making fuel alcohol needs a free federal TTB permit first; Oregon requires permits for graywater systems and composting toilets/privies; and burning needs a Josephine County burn permit and a burn day ((541) 476-9663).

When pulling, loop the chain above and below the ankle and pull one leg at a time. The calf should nurse within an hour. 🧰 Make-Do Household Guide How to make or replace everyday necessities when the store is gone — from basic supplies, things you can scavenge, and what grows around the Illinois Valley. Each section points to the detailed manuals in Homestead-Skills\ (especially Household-Make-Do\, Soap-Candles\ and Sanitation-Water\) and Electronics-Repair\. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - Never mix cleaning chemicals. Bleach + ammonia (or urine) makes toxic chloramine gas; bleach + vinegar or any acid makes chlorine gas. Use one product, rinse, then the next. - Lye (from ashes or the store) burns skin and blinds. Gloves and eye protection; flush any splash with plenty of water for 15 minutes. Never use aluminum pots with lye. - Label every container. Never store chemicals or fuel in food or drink bottles, and never reuse a container that held chemicals or fuel for food or water. - Never put gasoline in a lamp, stove or heater, and never burn charcoal, a camp stove or a generator indoors (carbon monoxide).

🧽 Cleaning and disinfecting - Most cleaning is just soap, hot water and scrubbing — it removes most germs along with the dirt. Homemade lye soap works fine (Soap-Candles\). - Scouring powder: baking soda, fine wood ash, or fine sand on a damp rag. - Glass and hard-water film: white vinegar mixed half and half with water (not on marble or stone, and never together with bleach). - Disinfecting with bleach (for kitchen surfaces, sickrooms, after flooding): plain unscented household bleach, 5 tablespoons (⅓ cup) per gallon of water, or 4 teaspoons per quart. Clean first, leave it wet for at least a minute, and mix it fresh every day — diluted bleach loses strength. Drinking water needs a much weaker dose — use the table in Water\EPA - Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water. - No bleach? Boiling water, scrubbing with soap, and drying things in full sun all kill germs.

👕 Laundry - Laundry soap: grate one bar of soap and mix with 1 cup washing soda (add 1 cup borax if you have it). Use 1–2 tablespoons per load, dissolved in hot water first. - Make washing soda from baking soda: spread baking soda in a pan and bake at 400 °F (200 °C) for about an hour, stirring now and then, until it turns dull and grainy. It's stronger than baking soda — wear gloves. - Ash water (old-time "lye wash"): soak hardwood ashes in water, let it settle, and use only the clear liquid for greasy or very dirty clothes. It's caustic — gloves, and never on wool or silk. - Washing by hand: soak overnight, agitate with a clean plunger in a bucket (or a washboard), rinse twice, wring hard, and dry in the sun — sunlight helps disinfect.

🪥 Personal care - Teeth: how you brush matters more than the paste. Brush twice a day with water, a little baking soda, or salt. No brush? Chew the end of a fresh green twig until it frays into bristles. Use thread as floss. (Medical\Manuals-PDF\Where There Is No Dentist) - Deodorant: wash daily; dust on baking soda or cornstarch (baking soda can irritate some skin). - Salve: melt 1 part beeswax with 4 parts oil or clean tallow (by weight) over low heat and pour into small tins. Lip balm is firmer: about 1 part wax to 2 parts oil. - Hair: wash with soap, then rinse with a cup of water with a spoonful of vinegar in it to remove soap film.

🩲 Menstrual pads and diapers - Reusable pads: several layers of absorbent cotton (old flannel or towel) sewn or folded into a pad, held in underwear. Rinse in cold water first, wash with soap, and dry in the sun. See Where Women Have No Doctor (Medical\). - Cloth diapers: absorbent cotton folded in layers, with a wool or plastic cover. Rinse, soak in a lidded bucket, wash hot with soap, dry in the sun.

🧻 Toilet paper alternatives - Water: a squeeze bottle of water, then wash your hands with soap — the cleanest option. - "Family cloth": cotton squares, used once, kept in a lidded bucket and washed hot, separately from other laundry. - Leaves: big soft thimbleberry leaves (common along roads and forest edges here in summer) or first-year mullein leaves. - ⚠️ Learn poison oak first — it's everywhere in the Illinois Valley. Leaves in threes, lobed like small oak leaves, shiny or dull, red in fall. The bare stems in winter still cause the rash. Also avoid stinging nettle.

🔥 Fire and light without stores - Fire starters: cotton balls rubbed with petroleum jelly; fatwood (resin-soaked heartwood from old pine or fir stumps — smells like turpentine and lights even when damp); dry bark and pine pitch. - Char cloth (catches a spark): put squares of 100% cotton cloth in a metal tin with a small nail hole in the lid, set it in a fire until smoke stops coming out, then let it cool before opening. - No matches: a ferro rod or flint-and-steel onto char cloth (steel struck on flint, quartz or pyrite throws sparks); a magnifying glass in sun; touching a 9-volt battery (or two AAs) to fine steel wool; or a bow drill — drill about ⅝ in thick and a foot long, of dry cedar, fir, cottonwood or basswood, on a board of the same wood with a notch cut to the center of the pit; tinder of dry grass with shredded cedar bark (Seton's Book of Woodcraft, pp. 192–194, and the Army survival manuals). - Oil lamp: a glass jar or tin, a wick of twisted cotton string or a cotton strip held up by a bent wire or a tin-lid holder, and any vegetable oil or melted fat. Keep the flame small. Never gasoline. Tallow candles: Soap-Candles\.

🪵 Glue, patching and waterproofing - Pine pitch glue: gently melt pine resin (it's flammable — heat beside the fire, not in it), stir in powdered charcoal (about 1 part to 3–4 parts resin) plus a pinch of fine plant fiber, and use while warm. Sets hard — for hafting tools, patching containers and seams. - Flour paste: cook flour and water to a thick paste — for paper and labels. - Waterproof cloth or leather: rub in beeswax, tallow or a beeswax–oil mix, then warm it so it soaks in.

👟 Clothing and footwear - Mending: running stitch for seams, backstitch where it must be strong, whipstitch for edges, and darning for holes (weave thread back and forth across the hole, then across the other way). Patch from the inside for strength. Needles from stiff wire; thread from unraveled fabric, dental floss or fishing line. - Sandals from old tires: trace your foot on tire tread, cut with a very sharp knife wetted with soapy water (steel belts make it slow — choose worn tread with no wire showing), sand the edges, and tie on with straps cut from an inner tube or with cord through slots. - Stay warm: wool keeps you warm even when wet; wet cotton pulls heat away — avoid it in cold rain.

🔧 Simple plumbing - Dripping faucet: shut the water off first, then replace the washer. A temporary washer can be cut from leather (cold taps) or rubber (hot taps). - Frozen pipe: open the faucet and thaw from the faucet end back toward the supply — never from the middle, where trapped water can burst the pipe. Thaw drains from the low end upward. (USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs.)

🔌 Electronics: repair and salvage Manuals are in Electronics-Repair\ (and device-by-device guides in the iFixit archive in Kiwix). Start with the Navy safety manual and the Kuphaldt multimeter and soldering guides. Safety first - Unplugged isn't safe. Capacitors hold a charge after unplugging. Discharge them with an insulated tool or shorting probe across the terminals and to the metal chassis, and recheck. - Microwave ovens can kill: the capacitor holds about 2,000 volts. Short it out before touching anything inside, never run the oven with the cover off, and don't break the magnetron's ceramic parts (toxic). Old tube TVs and monitors (CRTs) hold high voltage and can implode — leave them alone unless you know how. - Household 120 V can kill — especially with wet hands. Work with one hand when anything might be live. - Lithium batteries (laptops, phones, tools): throw out any that are swollen, dented, hot, or below about 2.5 volts. Charge only with a proper lithium charger, on a non-flammable surface, never unattended. Finding the fault — check the simple things first: power cord and plug, fuse, switch, batteries and their contacts, loose wires. Then measure voltages, then test parts. Test a part in the circuit before you desolder it. Bulging or leaking capacitors are the most common failure in power supplies and chargers. Multimeter quick tests - Continuity (beep): fuses, switches, cords, broken wires.

Multimeter quick tests - Continuity (beep): fuses, switches, cords, broken wires. - Diode: conducts one way only — about 0.5–0.7 V on the diode setting forward, nothing backward. Both ways = shorted; neither = open. - Transistor: test it like two diodes back to back (base-emitter, base-collector), and check collector-emitter reads high both ways. - Capacitor (discharged first): on the ohms setting a good one shows a brief "kick" then rising resistance; no kick = open, steady low reading = shorted. Resistor color code: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. Bands 1–2 are digits, band 3 is the number of zeros, the last band is tolerance (gold 5%, silver 10%). Example: yellow–violet–orange–gold = 47,000 Ω ±5%. Soldering: use rosin-core solder (never acid-core plumbing solder); a 25-watt iron for circuit boards. Make the wires hold mechanically first, heat the joint, not the solder, and don't move it while it cools. Remove old solder with copper wick or a solder sucker. What to salvage before throwing anything out: - Radios and clock radios: power transformers, cords, switches, knobs, speakers. - Computer power supplies: 12 V and 5 V power, fans, heat sinks, wire, connectors. - Printers and scanners: small

Radios and clock radios: power transformers, cords, switches, knobs, speakers. - Computer power supplies: 12 V and 5 V power, fans, heat sinks, wire, connectors. - Printers and scanners: small motors, gears, rods, belts, switches. - Microwaves (after discharging!): fan and turntable motors, door switches, fuses, magnets. - Cars: batteries, alternators (12 V charging), lights, wire, fuses, relays — see Army TM 9-8000 in Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals. - Also: LEDs, magnet wire from motors and transformers, fuses, batteries, cords. - Motor run capacitors can be reused; motor start capacitors can burst if used continuously. Crystal radio — no batteries needed (NBS Circular 120, 1922): a long wire antenna (about 75 ft, on insulators), a ground wire to a water pipe (never gas) or a rod in damp soil, a tuning coil wound on an oatmeal box, a germanium diode salvaged from an old radio as the detector, and a high-impedance earphone. It picks up AM stations with no power at all.

🍲 Hay-box cooking (saves fuel) Bring the pot to a full boil, then nest it tightly in hay, wool, newspaper or blankets in a box with a padded lid; it keeps cooking for hours on its own heat. Bring food back to a boil before eating if it has cooled below hot (food is safest kept above 140 °F).

🫙 Containers and storage - Food-grade buckets (recycling number 1 or 2 on the bottom, from bakeries and restaurants), glass jars and metal cans with lids. Wash with soap, then rinse with the bleach solution above. - Keep mice out: metal cans or glass; hang sacks from wire. Set snap traps along walls.

💧 Clean water from plastic bottles (SODIS) Fill clear plastic (PET) bottles of 2 liters or less with clear water, lay them on a roof or shiny surface in full sun for 6 hours (two full days if it's more than half cloudy). Doesn't work with cloudy water — let it settle or filter it first. Details: Sanitation-Water\ and Water\.

🐜 Pests - Roaches and ants: powdered borax mixed with sugar or flour, dusted into cracks (roaches), or a sponge soaked in borax-and-sugar syrup in their trail (ants). Keep borax away from children and pets. - Mosquitoes: screens, netting over beds, and smoke; homemade repellents are weak. - Lice: comb wet hair with a fine-tooth (nit) comb every day for two weeks; wash bedding hot. - Ticks: check every evening, especially after brush; pull straight out with tweezers.For hundreds more recipes — cleaners, polishes, glues, inks, waterproofing, pest control and home remedies — see the classic formula books in Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do\. They are old: use their methods, but follow the modern safety rules above, and skip any recipe using mercury (bichloride), arsenic, cyanide, lead, benzene, carbon tetrachloride or carbolic acid, or any "remedy" taken by mouth that contains kerosene — those are poisons. The safe staples in the same books are soap, washing soda, borax, vinegar and absorbent powders.

💊 Using found or expired medicines 1. Identify it. US pills must carry an imprint code. Open Pill-Identifier\PILL-IDENTIFIER.html, type the code, then check that the color, shape and size also match — the same code can be two different drugs (e.g. "I2" is ibuprofen 200 mg or amitriptyline 25 mg depending on size; "N 4" is nitroglycerin or a diet pill). No code at all = a supplement, a foreign or compounded product, or an illegal pill. 2. Never trust street pills. Pills that didn't come from a pharmacy can be counterfeits pressed with fentanyl — fake blue "M30" oxycodone, Xanax and Adderall are common, and many contain a deadly dose. 3. Look it up before giving it. In the WHO Model Formulary or MSF Essential Drugs (Medicines\), read what it treats, the dose, who must not take it, and interactions. For children, use the WHO Formulary for Children — children's doses go by weight. 4. Expired medicines. Most tablets and capsules kept sealed, cool and dry lose potency slowly — military testing extended most stockpiled lots by years, and some drugs kept 90% strength decades past their date. But: - Don't rely on expired or badly stored: insulin (lasts only ~28 days unrefrigerated; never use if it froze), nitroglycerin tablets (lose strength once opened — keep in the original glass bottle), epinephrine pens (weaker when expired — but an

only ~28 days unrefrigerated; never use if it froze), nitroglycerin tablets (lose strength once opened — keep in the original glass bottle), epinephrine pens (weaker when expired — but an expired pen with clear liquid is better than none in anaphylaxis), and mixed liquid antibiotics (amoxicillin suspension: 14 days in the fridge). - Throw out anything discolored, crumbling, sticky or smelling odd — especially tetracycline-family antibiotics, which can damage the kidneys when degraded. - Store medicines cool and dry (not the bathroom, kitchen or a car), in their original containers, out of children's reach. 5. The biggest dangers - Allergy — face or throat swelling, trouble breathing or widespread hives after a medicine is anaphylaxis: give epinephrine if you have it. - Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — no more than 4,000 mg a day for adults, counting every product; it's hidden in Norco, Vicodin, Percocet and many cold medicines. Too much causes liver failure. - Opioids — a dose that's normal for someone used to them can stop the breathing of someone who isn't, or of a child. Never combine with benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium, Klonopin), alcohol or other sedatives. Naloxone (Narcan) reverses opioid overdose — keep some. - Children — no cough/cold medicines under age 2, no aspirin for children or teens. - Interactions — check the formulary when someone already takes blood thinners, heart medicines or antidepressants. - Poisoning: Oregon Poison

medicines under age 2, no aspirin for children or teens. - Interactions — check the formulary when someone already takes blood thinners, heart medicines or antidepressants. - Poisoning: Oregon Poison Center 1-800-222-1222 (24/7, while phones work). Stock up now: ask your doctor about extra supplies of the medicines your household depends on, and keep an emergency kit (wound care, pain/fever medicine, antihistamines, oral rehydration salts, naloxone).
Ask an AI about the PDFs On a laptop, use the Library Assistant (searches everything, answers with sources), or GPT4All (AI-Offline\DocReader-GPT4All\) with the medical folders added as a collection.

Ham (Amateur), CB, Shortwave, GMRS/FRS & MURS — how they work and how to use them This guide explains, in plain language, how to communicate by radio when the internet and phones are down. It covers what each type of radio is, what it can do, which frequencies/channels matter in an emergency, and the basic procedures for calling for help. Legal note (normal times): Transmitting on ham (amateur) frequencies requires a license (easy to get — see below). GMRS requires a cheap license (no test). CB, FRS, MURS need no license. Shortwave listening needs no license (you're only receiving). In a genuine life-threatening emergency, FCC rules (47 CFR §97.405) let anyone use any means of radio to call for help. Listening is always legal. Learn and practice before you need it.

1. The quick version — what to grab and what to know | Need | Best tool | License | Range (typical) | | Talk to family nearby (same property / neighborhood) | FRS / GMRS walkie-talkie | FRS none; GMRS cheap | 0.5–2 mi (up to 5+ with GMRS + height) | | Talk across town / coordinate a group | GMRS (with repeater) or Ham VHF/UHF | GMRS cheap; Ham test | 5–50 mi via repeater | | Talk regionally / long distance / into other states | Ham HF | Ham (General class) | 100s–1000s mi | | Hear news & official broadcasts from anywhere | Shortwave receiver | none (listening) | Worldwide | | Road / vehicle convoy, truckers | CB | none | 1–15 mi | Three things everyone should know: 1. Monitor, don't just transmit. A cheap receiver tells you what's happening. 2. Higher antenna = more range. Antenna height matters more than watts. 3. Have a plan: agree on a channel/frequency and check-in times with your group in advance (write them down — see the card at the end).

2. How radio actually works (the 60-second version) - A radio turns your voice into radio waves at a certain frequency (measured in kilohertz kHz or megahertz MHz). Another radio tuned to the same frequency turns the wave back into sound. - Both radios must be on the same frequency/channel AND the same mode (e.g. FM, AM, SSB) to hear each other. - Only one person talks at a time. You press PTT (push-to-talk) to transmit, release it to listen. You cannot hear others while you hold PTT. - Frequency bands behave very differently: - VHF/UHF (high frequency numbers, ~30 MHz–3 GHz): travel in roughly straight "line of sight." Great locally, blocked by hills/buildings. Used by FRS, GMRS, MURS, and ham 2m/70cm. Extended by repeaters (see below). - HF / shortwave (low numbers, ~3–30 MHz): can bounce off the ionosphere and travel hundreds or thousands of miles ("skip"). Used by ham HF, CB (27 MHz), and shortwave broadcasters. Range changes with time of day and the sun.

3. CB Radio (Citizens Band) — no license, simple, vehicle-friendly - What it is: 40 channels around 27 MHz (in the HF band). No license needed. Cheap, everywhere, popular with truckers and off-roaders. - Range: usually 1–15 miles (more in flat/open terrain; occasionally hundreds of miles when "skip" conditions bounce signals off the ionosphere). - Power limit: 4 watts AM / 12 watts SSB (SSB radios reach farther). - Key channels: - Channel 9 — traditional emergency / help channel. - Channel 19 — highway / trucker channel (road conditions, traffic, convoys). - Channel 1–40 — general use; pick an unused one for your group. - Modes: Most CB is AM. Higher-end radios add SSB (USB/LSB) for more range — but both radios must use the same mode. - Good for: vehicle-to-vehicle, convoys, short local coordination with zero setup.
4. FRS / GMRS / MURS — the walkie-talkie families These are the little handheld radios ("walkie-talkies"). Great for family/group.

FRS (Family Radio Service) — no license - The blister-pack walkie-talkies. 22 channels in UHF (462/467 MHz). - Low power (0.5–2 W), fixed antenna. Range ~0.5–2 miles. - No license, no setup. Good for keeping a family/group in touch on foot.

GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service) — cheap license, no test - Shares channels with FRS but allows higher power (up to 50 W), detachable antennas, and repeaters — so range can reach 5–50+ miles via a repeater. - One GMRS license (~$35, no exam) covers your entire family for 10 years. - Best all-round family emergency radio: cheap, legal, powerful, easy.
MURS (Multi-Use Radio Service) — no license - 5 channels in VHF (151/154 MHz), up to 2 W. No license. - VHF often works better outdoors/rural than FRS/GMRS UHF. Good for property/farm.

5. Ham (Amateur) Radio — the serious emergency option Ham radio is the backbone of emergency communications. When everything else fails, hams relay health-and-welfare traffic, weather, and coordination across towns, states, and continents.

Licensing (USA) — easier than you think Three license levels, each a multiple-choice test (questions are public — you can study the exact pool): 1. Technician — entry level. Grants VHF/UHF (local, repeaters) plus some HF. Enough for local/regional emergency comms. ~1 evening of study. 2. General — adds most HF privileges → long-distance / cross-country. 3. Amateur Extra — full privileges. Get at least a Technician license now while it's easy, and ideally General so you can use HF for long distance. In a true emergency you may legally transmit without a license to save life/property — but you'll be far more effective if you've practiced.

The main ham bands and what they do - 2 meters (144–148 MHz, VHF) and 70 cm (420–450 MHz, UHF): local simplex + repeaters. Your everyday "talk around town" bands. - HF bands (e.g. 80m, 40m, 20m): long distance. - 40m (7 MHz): reliable regional (100s of miles), day and night — great for a state/region emergency net. - 20m (14 MHz): long-distance (cross-country / international) in daytime. - 80m (3.5 MHz): regional at night.

Repeaters — how hams get range from a handheld A repeater is a radio on a tower/hilltop that receives your weak signal and re-transmits it with a big antenna and power, massively extending range. To use one you set your radio to the repeater's output frequency, an offset (so it transmits on the input), and sometimes a CTCSS "tone." Local repeater lists (and emergency nets) are worth printing out for your area.
Simplex (radio-to-radio, no repeater) If repeaters are down, you talk simplex — directly, radio to radio, line of sight. The national 2m simplex calling frequency is 146.520 MHz.

Ham digital & data (advanced, FYI) Hams can also send text/email/images with no internet via Winlink (email over radio), FT8 (weak-signal), and APRS (position/text). Useful but needs more gear and practice.

6. Shortwave (SWL) — hearing the outside world - What it is: Using a shortwave receiver to listen to broadcasts on the HF bands (roughly 1.8–30 MHz). No license needed to listen. - Why it matters: When local media and internet are down, shortwave lets you hear international news, government/emergency broadcasts, and ham traffic from far away — because HF signals bounce worldwide. - What to listen for: - International broadcasters (news from outside the affected area). - NOAA Weather Radio (VHF 162.400–162.550 MHz) — continuous US weather & emergency alerts. Every emergency kit should have a NOAA weather radio. - Ham bands (40m/20m) — to hear emergency nets and relays. - AM/FM broadcast and Emergency Alert System (EAS) on a normal radio. - Modes: Broadcasts are usually AM; ham/utility voice is often SSB (USB/LSB). A radio with SSB hears far more. - Tip: A simple long wire antenna dramatically improves shortwave reception.

7. Antennas, power & range (the practical stuff) - Antenna height beats power. Getting the antenna up high (roof, tree, mast) adds more range than buying a bigger amplifier. - Use the right antenna for the band. A proper resonant antenna (correct length for the frequency) works far better than a random wire. - Line of sight (VHF/UHF): range ≈ limited by the horizon and obstructions. Height = range. Repeaters overcome this. - HF skip: range changes with the time of day and solar conditions. Lower bands (80m) are better at night; higher bands (20m) are better in daytime. - Power: keep radios charged. Stock spare batteries, a 12V battery, a solar panel, and car-charging cables. A radio with a dead battery is a paperweight. - Grounding & safety: never put an antenna where it can touch power lines; ground equipment to reduce static/lightning risk.

8. How to call for help (procedure) 1. Listen first. Make sure you're not interrupting other emergency traffic. 2. Use the emergency call: - Voice distress: say "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY" (life-threatening) or "PAN-PAN" (urgent but not immediately life-threatening), then your info. - On CB, call on Channel 9. On ham, break into the local emergency net or call on a repeater / 146.520 simplex. 3. Give the essentials — slowly, clearly, repeat: - Who you are (name / call sign). - Where you are (address, cross-streets, GPS coords, landmarks). - What the emergency is (injury, fire, trapped, etc.). - What you need (medical, rescue, relay a message). 4. Spell hard words with the phonetic alphabet (below). 5. Stay on, don't wander off frequency. Keep the radio on so responders can call back. Repeat your message at intervals if no answer.

NATO phonetic alphabet Alpha Bravo Charlie Delta Echo Foxtrot Golf Hotel India Juliet Kilo Lima Mike November Oscar Papa Quebec Romeo Sierra Tango Uniform Victor Whiskey X-ray Yankee Zulu. Numbers: say digits individually ("one-two-zero").

Common "pro-words" - "Over" = I'm done talking, your turn. - "Out" = conversation finished (don't say "over and out"). - "Roger" / "Copy" = I received and understand. - "Say again" = repeat (don't say "repeat"). - "Affirmative / Negative" = yes / no. - "Break" = pause / someone with emergency traffic wants in.

9. A sensible emergency radio kit (shopping / checklist) - [ ] NOAA weather radio (hand-crank/solar + battery) — alerts & forecasts. - [ ] Shortwave receiver with SSB — hear news & ham traffic worldwide (RX only). - [ ] A pair+ of GMRS radios (and a GMRS license) — family/group, best bang for buck. FRS works with no license at shorter range. - [ ] A dual-band (2m/70cm) ham handheld (HT) — cheap; huge capability with a Technician license. Add a better antenna. - [ ] (Advanced) An HF ham radio + General license — true long distance. - [ ] CB if you travel by vehicle/convoy. - [ ] Power: spare batteries, 12V battery, solar panel, car charger. - [ ] Better antennas + coax; a roll of wire for an HF/long-wire antenna. - [ ] Printed frequency card (below), local repeater list, notebook & pencil.

10. Print-and-keep frequency card Fill in your group's agreed channels and local repeaters, then print this page. ===================== EMERGENCY RADIO CARD ===================== Our group PRIMARY channel : _______________ Mode: _______ Our group BACKUP channel : _______________ Mode: _______ Check-in times (daily) : _______ _______ _______ CB emergency / help ....... Channel 9 CB highway / travel ....... Channel 19 Ham 2m simplex calling .... 146.520 MHz (FM) NOAA Weather Radio ........ 162.400 / 162.425 / 162.450 / 162.475 / 162.500 / 162.525 / 162.550 MHz FRS/GMRS family channel ... _______ (GMRS license #: __________) Local repeaters (output / offset / tone): 1) ________ MHz / ____ / tone ______ (____________) 2) ________ MHz / ____ / tone ______ (____________) 3) ________ MHz / ____ / tone ______ (____________) Distress voice: "MAYDAY x3" (life threat) or "PAN-PAN x3" (urgent) Say: WHO you are - WHERE you are - WHAT's wrong - WHAT you need ==================================================================

11. Where to learn more offline (already in this kit) - Appropedia and iFixit archives (in E:\Manuals\, via the Kiwix reader) include antenna, electronics and repair articles. - WikiMed / Wikipedia-medicine (E:\Medical\) for treating injuries while you wait for help. - Study the ham license question pools (download them now while you have internet; the exact questions and answers are public) so you can get licensed quickly. Practice now: tune around, learn your radios' menus, program the channels above, and do a test check-in with your group. Skills and muscle memory matter more than gear.
